A.explanation: Sound waves spread around the corner of the building into the shadow region where S stands, which is diffraction.

B.explanation: Interference needs two coherent sources overlapping to form maxima and minima, not a single sound spreading around one corner.

C.explanation: Polarisation only applies to transverse waves and describes oscillation direction, and sound in air is longitudinal so cannot be polarised.

D.explanation: Reflection needs another surface to bounce the wave back, but the question states there are no other structures nearby.

hints: Notice in the diagram that the straight-line path from R to S is blocked by the solid building, so S is in the sound shadow with no direct wave.
Recall that sound in air has wavelength of order $0.3 \text{ m}$ to $2 \text{ m}$, which is large enough to spread significantly around a building corner.
Connect spreading of a wave around an obstacle or through a gap into a shadow region to the named wave effect, and check why bouncing off another wall cannot apply here.
walkthrough: Look at the diagram: R is above the building and S is at the side, so the solid building blocks any direct straight-line travel of sound from R to S.
State the rule: when a wave meets an obstacle or edge, it spreads out beyond the edge into the geometrical shadow. This spreading is called diffraction.
Apply it here: sound waves from R reach the corner of the building and diffract around it, so wave energy reaches S even though there is no line of sight.

Check the size effect: significant diffraction occurs when wavelength $\lambda$ is comparable to the obstacle size. Audible sound with speed about $340 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and frequency $170$ to $1000 \text{ Hz}$ gives $\lambda = v/f$ of about $0.34 \text{ m}$ to $2.0 \text{ m}$, so spreading around a corner is strong.

Rule out the other effects: reflection would need a second nearby wall to bounce from, interference would need superposition of two coherent waves, and polarisation cannot occur for longitudinal sound waves.
Therefore the hearing around the corner is best explained by diffraction. This is option A
